title: Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission
subtitle: Unlocking India's Tribal Forest Economy
body_text:
Many of India's 10.4 crore Scheduled Tribes derive 20–40% of their annual income from Minor Forest Produce (MFP). Historically, tribals sold this produce to middlemen at distress prices, earning below the cost of their own labour. To address this, the government runs the Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission (PMJVM). The mission organises tribals into community-owned Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (VDVKs), moving them from raw produce sellers to value-adding entrepreneurs . So far, 4,172 VDVKs have been sanctioned, linking 12.48 lakh tribal members to the scheme. The government also buys MFP at a pre-determined Minimum Support Price (MSP). PMJVM provides enterprise funding and helps tribals access markets through fairs, e-commerce platforms, and exhibitions.
Protecting Tribal Forest Economies
For millions of forest-dwelling tribal families, Minor Forest Produce (MFP)—such as honey, tendu leaves, mahua flowers, tamarind, lac, bamboo and wild herbs —is not merely a forest resource. It is a primary source of livelihood. About 20% to 40% of their annual income is from selling MFP. Yet, despite directly procuring and selling MFP, tribals receive only a fraction of its market value. This is because they often sell MFP to intermediaries at low prices.
The Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission (PMJVM) seeks to change this equation. Launched in 2021-22, the Mission provides a systematic way for them to improve MFP’s value by skilling the tribals in newer technology and practices . The scheme links the communities to the larger national and digital markets to help them get more exposure and sell more products. It also guarantees Minimum Support Prices (MSP) to tribals by directly procuring the produce from them.
These efforts are helping forest gatherers become owners of their community enterprises while strengthening India's tribal economy at the grassroots level.
Minor Forest Products & Minimum Support Price While the government manages most of India’s forests to preserve ecology and wildlife, tribals and other traditional forest-dwelling communities are given access to these areas for the preservation of their livelihoods. In 2006, the government enacted the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act — also called the Forest Rights Act . The Act defines minor forest produce as “ all non-timber forest produce of plant origin including bamboo, brush wood, stumps, cane, tussar, cocoons, honey, wax, lac, tendu or kendu leaves, medicinal plants and herbs, roots, tubers and the like ." The government has notified Minimum Support Price for 87 MFP items under PMJVM . The Forest Rights Act recognises that forest-dwelling communities have historically depended on forest products for sustenance and livelihood. The Act gives tribals rights to procure and sell non-timber minor forest produce. Separately, the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act (1996) grants tribal Gram Panchayats ownership rights over minor forest produce. The Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation of India (TRIFED) , mandated with the marketing and development of tribal products, purchases non-timber forest produce at the pre-determined price (MSP) regardless of the market price of the product. It does so through a network of state implementing agencies — including tribal development cooperatives and forest development corporations. Since 2013–14, state governments have procured 2,67,954 metric tonnes of MFPs worth Rs. 693.98 crore under the scheme.
How Does PMJVM Support Tribals?
Beyond MSP procurement, the PVJM scheme also provides skilling, technological, marketing, and infrastructural support to tribals.
Organising Tribals into Van Dhan Vikas Kendras
The Mission mobilises tribal gatherers into self-help groups (SHGs). A group of 15 SHGs, comprising about 300 tribals , are clustered together into one Van Dhan Vikas Kendra (VDVK). At least 60% of VDVK members must be from Scheduled Tribe communities.
The Van Dhan Yojana , launched on April 14, 2018, is a part of PMJVM. It forms the foundation of the VDVK model and powers its implementation across tribal communities.
Skilling, Funding and Technological Support
The Government organises skilling and other training programmes for MFP gatherers, including trainings on scientific harvesting practices, at Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (VDVKs).
The SHGs are also provided with:
Infrastructural support , established in a beneficiary's home or a government or gram panchayat building Primary processing equipment — cutting and sieving tools, decorticators, dryers, and packaging tools — based on locally available MFPs Training for 30 members on sustainable harvesting and value addition, with raw materials and trainee kits provided Working capital , facilitated through tie-ups with financial institutions, banks, and the National Scheduled Tribes Finance and Development Corporation (NSTFDC) Storage and transportation support on a rental basis.
Marketing and Business Support
Apart from value addition, VDVKs are also centres for market linkages – both local and distant – for the final products.
VDVKs are established around local Haat Bazaars , the primary MFP procurement points, to make it easier for tribals to sell products they produce. There are over 5,000 Haats in tribal areas . Haats are being modernised in a phased manner— with permanent structures, storage, drinking water, shade, and weighing equipment. VDVKs may partner with private entities or non-profits for value addition or marketing of their products. TRIFED disseminates market intelligence — including daily rates and e-commerce avenues —to VDVKs to improve their decision-making on business deals. PMJVM also provides: Branding, promotion, and advertisement of tribal products through festivals, exhibitions, and artisan melas Geo-tagging of VDVKs and other scheme assets Geographical Indicators for tribal produce (GI is a sign used on products that have a specific geographical origin and possess qualities or a reputation that are due to that origin) Building and upgrading IT and e-commerce platforms Research and development support
Under the PMJVM scheme:
4,172 VDVKs have been sanctioned and 2,911 VDVKs are functional , with reported sales of around Rs. 168 crores (as on July 31, 2026). 12.48 lakh tribal members have been linked to the VDVKs.
VDVKs Help in Tribal Women Empowerment Most collections and sales are carried out by women, making PMJVM a key instrument of tribal women's financial empowerment. The Nyigamane, Ho Yorbe, Medumhagdum VDVK in Arunachal Pradesh ’s Leparada district was established in October 2021 with 300 women SHG members and farmers . This VDVK converts locally available non-timber forest and agricultural produce into processed, marketable goods. The products created are: King Chilli Pickle from King Chillis (Bhut Jolokia — a north eastern Indian specialty) Bamboo Shoot Pickle from bamboo shoots (a common MFP in north-eastern India) Turmeric Powder from locally grown turmeric Ginger Powder from locally grown ginger Pineapple Jam from Pineapples (abundant in Arunachal Pradesh) Pineapple Squash from Pineapples Orange Squash from Oranges The VDVK has sold Rs. 11 lakh worth of these products from 2022-23 onwards. It has empowered the women, who no longer need to depend on only seasonable agriculture for income throughout the year. The women jointly own the business – they are not mere workers but also have a stake in the brand and the enterprise.
Towards A Sustainable Forest Economy
Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission (PMJVM) provides livelihood opportunities to forest-dwelling tribals, offering a systematic way to produce and market non-timber forest produce. These products are locally sourced and rooted in traditional practices — representing a forest-based economy balancing community ownership with market competitiveness.
In a world increasingly driven by mass-manufactured and plastic-packaged goods, they are India's distinctive offering: natural, community-owned, and forest-born . PMJVM embodies Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikaas - ensuring India's growth story reaches its most remote forests and the communities who call them home. This will eventually contribute to India’s vision of a Viksit Bharat@2047 .

enrichment.summary: This PIB backgrounder explains the Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission (PMJVM), launched in 2021-22, which aims to convert tribal Minor Forest Produce (MFP) gatherers into value-adding entrepreneurs through community-owned Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (VDVKs). As of the release, 4,172 VDVKs have been sanctioned (2,911 functional) linking 12.48 lakh tribal members, with MSP notified for 87 MFP items and cumulative procurement of 2,67,954 metric tonnes worth Rs. 693.98 crore since 2013-14. The scheme provides skilling, processing equipment, working capital, market linkages, branding and e-commerce support, and is implemented through TRIFED and state agencies.
enrichment.context:
Minor Forest Produce constitutes 20-40% of annual income for many of India's Scheduled Tribes, who have historically been forced to sell to middlemen at distress prices. PMJVM builds on two earlier legal foundations: the Forest Rights Act (2006), which recognises forest-dwellers' rights to collect and sell non-timber forest produce, and PESA (1996), which vests ownership of MFP in tribal Gram Panchayats in Scheduled Areas. The Van Dhan Yojana (2018) forms the operational backbone of PMJVM, organising tribal gatherers into SHGs clustered into VDVKs (about 300 members each, 60% ST). TRIFED's MSP mechanism for MFP is designed to insulate tribal incomes from market price volatility by guaranteeing a floor price regardless of market conditions.

This release is a fairly detailed scheme explainer with concrete implementation figures (VDVK numbers, sales figures, MSP-covered items) and ties together multiple related legal/institutional frameworks (FRA, PESA, TRIFED, NSTFDC), making it useful revision material for tribal welfare and social justice topics, though it is a routine backgrounder rather than a new policy announcement.

prelims_questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission (PMJVM):
1. It guarantees Minimum Support Price for Minor Forest Produce items.
2. Van Dhan Vikas Kendras must have at least 60% membership from Scheduled Tribes.
3. The scheme was launched under the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: PMJVM guarantees MSP for notified MFP items and mandates at least 60% ST membership in VDVKs. However, PMJVM was launched in 2021-22 as a government mission, not under PESA 1996, which is a separate law granting Gram Panchayats ownership of MFP.

prelims_questions.question: The term 'Minor Forest Produce' as defined under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 includes all of the following EXCEPT:
prelims_questions.explanation: The Forest Rights Act defines Minor Forest Produce as non-timber forest produce of plant origin, explicitly excluding timber; it includes items like bamboo, tendu leaves, honey, wax and lac.

mains_questions.question: Discuss how the Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission seeks to transform tribal communities from raw produce sellers into value-adding entrepreneurs. Examine the institutional and legal framework (Forest Rights Act, PESA, TRIFED) that supports this transformation.

Minor Forest Produce constitutes a significant share of tribal household income in India. Critically evaluate the effectiveness of Minimum Support Price mechanisms in protecting tribal livelihoods against market exploitation.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a strong factual core (VDVK structure, MSP-covered MFP items, legal foundations under FRA/PESA, Van Dhan Yojana) that is highly testable as objective questions, while also offering substantive analytical material on tribal livelihood security, women's economic empowerment and implementation gaps that would support a Mains answer on social justice or welfare schemes.

prelims.point: A Van Dhan Vikas Kendra (VDVK) comprises 15 SHGs (~300 tribal members), of which at least 60% must be Scheduled Tribe members
prelims.why_important: The specific numerical composition (15 SHGs, 300 members, 60% ST) is a classic detail UPSC uses to test scheme architecture.

prelims.point: MSP has been notified for 87 Minor Forest Produce (MFP) items under PMJVM, procured by TRIFED and state agencies
prelims.why_important: The MSP item count and the procuring agency (TRIFED) are precise, testable facts distinguishing this scheme from general agricultural MSP mechanisms.

prelims.point: The Forest Rights Act (2006) legally defines 'Minor Forest Produce' as non-timber forest produce of plant origin (bamboo, tendu leaves, honey, lac, medicinal herbs, etc.)
prelims.why_important: UPSC often tests statutory definitions verbatim to check whether aspirants confuse MFP with timber or non-plant produce.

prelims.point: The Van Dhan Yojana was launched on 14 April 2018 and forms the operational foundation of PMJVM (launched 2021-22)
prelims.why_important: Chronology and the parent-scheme relationship (Van Dhan Yojana nested within PMJVM) is a common prelims trap on scheme lineage.

mains.point: MFP contributes 20-40% of annual income for many Scheduled Tribes, who historically sold to middlemen at distress prices below the cost of labour
mains.analytical_use: Useful to establish the problem statement in a question on tribal economic exploitation or the rationale for MSP-based interventions.

mains.point: Only 2,911 of 4,172 sanctioned VDVKs are functional, indicating an implementation gap between sanction and ground-level operationalisation
mains.analytical_use: Can be cited in a 'critically examine' question on gaps between scheme design and delivery for tribal welfare programmes.

mains.point: Most VDVK collection and sales activities are carried out by women, making PMJVM an instrument of tribal women's financial empowerment and joint enterprise ownership
mains.analytical_use: Supports answers on women's economic empowerment through community enterprise models, distinct from mere wage employment.

mains.point: PMJVM shifts tribals from raw MFP sellers to value-adding entrepreneurs via skilling, processing equipment, branding, GI tagging and e-commerce linkages
mains.theme: Value chain development and market integration
mains.analytical_use: Useful for 'suggest measures' questions on strengthening forest-based rural/tribal economies through value addition rather than raw extraction.

both.concept: TRIFED's MSP mechanism for MFP, which guarantees a floor price regardless of market fluctuation and has procured 2,67,954 MT worth Rs. 693.98 crore since 2013-14
both.prelims_angle: UPSC could ask which agency administers MFP-MSP, since when, or the cumulative procurement figures.
both.mains_angle: The mechanism can be analysed as a market-failure correction tool insulating vulnerable forest-dependent communities from price volatility and middleman exploitation.

both.concept: The distinct legal bases of FRA (2006, individual/community right to collect and sell MFP) and PESA (1996, ownership of MFP vested in Gram Panchayats in Scheduled Areas)
both.prelims_angle: UPSC could test which Act grants which specific right — collection/sale rights (FRA) versus ownership (PESA) — a classic distinction-based question.
both.mains_angle: This layered legal architecture can be examined for its implications on tribal self-governance, local body empowerment, and potential conflicts between state agencies and Gram Panchayat authority over MFP.

low_priority.point: The Arunachal Pradesh Nyigamane VDVK case study on King Chilli pickle, bamboo shoot pickle and pineapple products
low_priority.reason: An illustrative anecdote with no independently testable fact or generalisable analytical claim beyond the scheme's stated objectives.

low_priority.point: Slogans such as 'Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikaas' and 'Viksit Bharat@2047'
low_priority.reason: Political framing rhetoric with no policy substance or testable content.

low_priority.point: Modernisation of over 5,000 Haat Bazaars with permanent structures, storage and weighing equipment
low_priority.reason: Minor administrative/infrastructural detail without significance beyond context.
